figures.name: Ignatius of Antioch
figures.dates: died c. 107-117 (martyred at Rome under Trajan; the exact year is unknown)
figures.places: Antioch in Syria (bishop); taken under guard through Asia Minor (Philadelphia, Smyrna, Troas) to Rome
figures.role: Bishop of Antioch, the second after Peter by Eusebius's count; condemned to the beasts; wrote seven letters on the road to his death
figures.status_note: Saint in the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox churches, and commemorated by Anglicans and Lutherans (17 October in the West, 20 December in the East). Caution: only seven letters are his (the "middle recension": Ephesians, Magnesians, Trallians, Romans, Philadelphians, Smyrnaeans, Polycarp). A padded "longer recension" of the same letters and six extra letters (Tarsians, Antiochians, Hero, Philippians, Mary at Neapolis, and more) were forged or interpolated around the 4th century, and the letters to St John and the Virgin Mary are medieval Latin. A minority of scholars date even the seven later than Trajan. His letters speak harshly of Christians who keep Jewish customs ("Judaizing"), and he counsels slaves not to seek freedom at church expense: both need care with a modern reader. The "Martyrdom of Ignatius" (his trial before Trajan) is a later legendary text, not an eyewitness record.
figures.hook: Chained to ten soldiers he called "leopards" on the long road from Syria to the lions at Rome, he wrote ahead to the Roman Christians begging them not to save him.

stories.story: Marched from Antioch to Rome under a military guard, he compared his escort to wild animals: "ten leopards, I mean a band of soldiers", who got worse the more kindly they were treated. He said he was already fighting beasts "both by land and sea, both by night and day".

He feared the Roman Christians would use their influence to get him released, and wrote ahead to stop them: "Allow me to become food for the wild beasts... I am the wheat of God." He even said that if the beasts held back, "I will compel them to do so." The letter is dated at its end, "on the twenty-third day of August", written from Smyrna.
stories.source: Letter to the Romans, chapters 1-5 and 10

stories.story: At Philadelphia some people told him, "If I do not find it in the ancient Scriptures, I will not believe the Gospel." When he answered "It is written", they shot back, "That remains to be proved." His reply: "to me Jesus Christ is in the place of all that is ancient."

In the church at Philadelphia he suddenly shouted, "with a loud voice: Give heed to the bishop, and to the presbytery and deacons." Some suspected he had been tipped off about a split in the congregation. He insisted no one had told him: the Spirit had.

Polycarp of Smyrna, who met him on the road, gathered his letters and sent copies to the church at Philippi, telling them that the letters "comprise faith and patience, and every kind of edification". Irenaeus, a generation later, quoted his "I am God's wheat" line.
stories.source: Eusebius, Church History 3.36 (quoting Polycarp, Letter to the Philippians 13, and Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.28.4)

stories.story: Legend, recorded about 330 years later: the church historian Socrates says Ignatius "saw a vision of angels hymning in alternate chants the Holy Trinity" and brought this back-and-forth (antiphonal) singing into the church at Antioch. Treat as tradition, not history.

John Chrysostom, preaching in Antioch about 280 years later, told how the cities along the road carried Ignatius's remains home on their shoulders "as with a noble athlete", and said Antioch "sent forth a Bishop, and received a martyr".
stories.source: John Chrysostom, Homily on St Ignatius 5 (c. 388)

temperament.trait: Burning, almost impatient longing to die for Christ
temperament.evidence: He prays the beasts will be "eager to rush upon me", and says he will coax them to devour him speedily; "Pardon me [in this]: I know what is for my benefit."

temperament.trait: Humble to the point of self-reproach
temperament.evidence: "I am ashamed to be counted one of them; for indeed I am not worthy, as being the very last of them, and one born out of due time." He repeatedly calls himself "a condemned man" and not yet a real disciple.
temperament.source: Letter to the Romans, chapters 4 and 9; Letter to the Ephesians, chapters 3 and 12

temperament.trait: Wary of his own pride and of flattery
temperament.evidence: "I have great knowledge in God, but I restrain myself, lest, I should perish through boasting... For they that speak to me [in the way of commendation] scourge me."

temperament.trait: Vehement and loud when unity is at stake
temperament.evidence: "when I was among you, I cried, I spoke with a loud voice: Give heed to the bishop." He calls himself "a man devoted to unity".

temperament.trait: Affectionate; names his friends one by one
temperament.evidence: He closes letters with personal greetings: "I salute Alce, my dearly beloved", "the wife of Epitropus, with all her house and children", "Attalus, my beloved".
temperament.source: Letter to Polycarp, chapter 8; Letter to the Smyrnaeans, chapter 13

temperament.trait: Gentle toward opponents in theory, fierce in language
temperament.evidence: He tells Christians to answer hostility with meekness and prayer (Ephesians 10), yet calls false teachers "ravening dogs, who bite secretly" and "beasts in the shape of men".
temperament.source: Letter to the Ephesians, chapters 7 and 10; Letter to the Smyrnaeans, chapter 4

temperament.trait: Remembered (much later) as mild and even-tempered
temperament.evidence: Chrysostom, preaching in his city nearly three centuries on, says he matched Paul's picture of a bishop: "neither self-willed, nor soon angry, nor given to wine, nor a striker, but gentle, not contentious, no lover of money". This is a later preacher's praise, not an eyewitness.
temperament.source: John Chrysostom, Homily on St Ignatius 2

genuine_lines.quote: I am the wheat of God, and let me be ground by the teeth of the wild beasts, that I may be found the pure bread of Christ.
genuine_lines.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: It is better for a man to be silent and be [a Christian], than to talk and not to be one.
genuine_lines.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Every kind of wound is not healed with the same plaster.
genuine_lines.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: For the beginning is faith, and the end is love.
genuine_lines.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: My love has been crucified, and there is no fire in me desiring to be fed; but there is within me a water that lives and speaks, saying to me inwardly, Come to the Father.
genuine_lines.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Stand firm, as does an anvil which is beaten. It is the part of a noble athlete to be wounded, and yet to conquer.
genuine_lines.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Wherever the bishop shall appear, there let the multitude [of the people] also be; even as, wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church.
genuine_lines.location: chapter 8 (the earliest surviving use of "the Catholic Church")
genuine_lines.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: For Christianity did not embrace Judaism, but Judaism Christianity
genuine_lines.location: chapter 10 (among the earliest uses of the word "Christianity")
genuine_lines.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: breaking one and the same bread, which is the medicine of immortality, and the antidote to prevent us from dying
genuine_lines.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent

misattributed.line: "If any one fasts on the Lord's Day or on the Sabbath, except on the paschal Sabbath only, he is a murderer of Christ."
misattributed.truth: From the spurious Letter to the Philippians (chapter 13), one of the letters forged under his name around the 4th century. Printed among the "Spurious Epistles" at newadvent.org/fathers/0114.htm.

misattributed.line: "Let no one among you be idle; for idleness is the mother of want."
misattributed.truth: From the spurious Letter to the Tarsians (chapter 9), not one of the seven genuine letters.

misattributed.line: "Keep God in remembrance, and you shall never sin."
misattributed.truth: From the spurious Letter to Hero (chapter 7).

misattributed.line: "Where the bishop is, there is the Church."
misattributed.truth: A popular compression. The genuine line (Smyrnaeans 8) is: "Wherever the bishop shall appear, there let the multitude [of the people] also be; even as, wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church." It says the people should gather where the bishop is; it does not define the Church as the bishop.

misattributed.line: Letters of Ignatius to St John the Apostle and to the Virgin Mary (and her reply)
misattributed.truth: Medieval Latin forgeries, printed as spurious in the Ante-Nicene Fathers.

misattributed.line: Sayings in the "longer recension" of the seven letters (for example the longer Magnesians 9 telling Christians to "keep the Sabbath after a spiritual manner")
misattributed.truth: The longer recension is a 4th-century expansion. Quote only the shorter (middle) recension, which is what New Advent prints for the seven letters.

misattributed.line: Legend: Ignatius was the child Jesus took in His arms (Matthew 18:2)
misattributed.truth: A later Greek tradition. John Chrysostom, preaching in Antioch c. 388, says the opposite: Ignatius "had not even seen him, nor enjoyed his companionship" (Homily on St Ignatius 4).

misattributed.line: Legend: his heart was found inscribed with the name of Jesus
misattributed.truth: A medieval embellishment (it appears in the 13th-century Golden Legend); nothing in the early sources. Secondary knowledge, not re-checked in a primary text here.

misattributed.line: His dialogue with Trajan ("Who is Theophorus?" "He who has Christ within his breast.")
misattributed.truth: From the "Martyrdom of Ignatius" (Martyrium Colbertinum), a later legendary account, not a contemporary record. Good story, weak history.

opinions.position: Skipping the gathered church is pride; a believer who stays away condemns himself.
opinions.side_note: Related to "solitude": he values the assembled church over private faith.
opinions.quote: He, therefore, that does not assemble with the Church, has even by this manifested his pride, and condemned himself.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Sharply split. Many people today, including many Christians, say you can follow Jesus fine without church; weekly attenders and Catholic, Orthodox and evangelical leaders would agree with Ignatius. A strong, clean statement for a quiz.

opinions.position: Christians should gather often to give thanks; frequent meeting breaks the power of evil.
opinions.quote: Take heed, then, often to come together to give thanks to God, and show forth His praise. For when you assemble frequently in the same place, the powers of Satan are destroyed
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most churchgoers agree in principle; less-committed people see it as optional. Overlaps with the item above.

opinions.position: Do nothing in church life without the bishop; honour him as you would the Lord.
opinions.side_note: Among the strongest pro-authority voices of the early Church.
opinions.quote: Let no man do anything connected with the Church without the bishop.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split along church lines: Catholic and Orthodox readers largely agree; many Protestants and most non-religious people would reject deferring to a church leader in everything.

opinions.position: Do not try to escape martyrdom, and do not let friends rescue you: dying for Christ is how you reach God.
opinions.side_note: Side: do not flee. He goes further than most, asking others not to intervene.
opinions.quote: Pray, then, do not seek to confer any greater favour upon me than that I be sacrificed to God while the altar is still prepared
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Almost everyone today would flee or accept rescue, and many would find eagerness for death troubling. Later Fathers (Cyprian, Athanasius) defended flight. Good as a sparring point, one-sided today.

opinions.position: Being a Christian quietly beats talking about it without living it; a silent leader deserves more respect, not less.
opinions.side_note: Pro-silence.
opinions.quote: Now the more any one sees the bishop keeping silence, the more ought he to revere him.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Many admire quiet leaders; many others want leaders who speak up and explain themselves. A genuine split.

opinions.position: Loving easy people earns no credit; win the difficult ones by gentleness, and fit the remedy to the person.
opinions.side_note: Gentle, case-by-case correction.
opinions.quote: If you love the good disciples, no thanks are due to you on that account; but rather seek by meekness to subdue the more troublesome.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Widely agreed in theory; some prefer firm, uniform rules over tailoring. Mild split.

opinions.position: Answer anger with meekness, boasting with humility, insults with prayer, cruelty with gentleness.
opinions.side_note: Against returning anger.
opinions.quote: Be meek in response to their wrath, humble in opposition to their boasting: to their blasphemies return your prayers
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Many admire it but think some anger at injustice is right and needed; a real split between "turn the other cheek" and "righteous anger" people.

opinions.position: Freedom from anger is a mark of godliness; God is not found where there is division and wrath.
opinions.side_note: Against anger.
opinions.quote: For where there is division and wrath, God does not dwell.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split as above.

opinions.position: Lifelong celibacy is good for those who can keep it, but the moment you boast about it you are ruined.
opinions.side_note: Pro-celibacy, anti-pride.
opinions.quote: If any one can continue in a state of purity, to the honour of Him who is Lord of the flesh, let him so remain without boasting. If he begins to boast, he is undone
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Few today see celibacy as a higher way; Catholics and Orthodox honour it for some. The warning against spiritual pride is widely agreed.

opinions.position: Couples should marry with the approval of the bishop, so that the marriage is "according to God, and not after their own lust".
opinions.side_note: The church has a say in who marries whom.
opinions.quote: But it becomes both men and women who marry, to form their union with the approval of the bishop, that their marriage may be according to God, and not after their own lust.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today would reject a church leader approving their choice of spouse; some traditional communities still seek a pastor's blessing. Split, leaning against.

opinions.position: The pleasures of this life no longer delight him; he wants only God.
opinions.side_note: Against enjoyment (spoken as a man about to die).
opinions.quote: I have no delight in corruptible food, nor in the pleasures of this life.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people, Christians included, think enjoying food and life is good. Note the context: a prisoner facing death.

opinions.position: Do not receive people who teach falsehood about Christ, and if possible do not even meet them; just pray for them.
opinions.side_note: Contrasts with Justin, who debated opponents at length, and with Irenaeus's "stretch out the hand".
opinions.quote: whom you must not only not receive, but, if it be possible, not even meet with; only you must pray to God for them
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Strongly split: most people today value hearing all views; some Christians practise separation from false teachers.

opinions.position: If God paid us according to our works, we would cease to exist; we live by His kindness.
opinions.side_note: Side: grace.
opinions.quote: For were He to reward us according to our works, we should cease to be.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Christians broadly agree in words; many ordinary people believe good people earn a good afterlife. Useful split.

opinions.position: Teaching is good only if the teacher lives it; Christians are known by what they do, not what they profess.
opinions.quote: It is good to teach, if he who speaks also acts.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Nearly everyone agrees; one-sided, so weak as a quiz item on its own.

opinions.position: He would not rest faith on winning an argument from old documents: Christ himself, crucified and risen, is the only "archive" he needs.
opinions.side_note: Side: faith does not wait on proof-texts.
opinions.quote: But to me Jesus Christ is in the place of all that is ancient: His cross, and death, and resurrection, and the faith which is by Him, are undefiled monuments of antiquity
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many want evidence and argument first; others say faith rests on Christ, not on proofs.

opinions.position: Those who repent and come back into the unity of the church belong to God; the Lord forgives all who repent.
opinions.side_note: Side: yes, with return to the community and its bishop.
opinions.quote: To all them that repent, the Lord grants forgiveness, if they turn in penitence to the unity of God, and to communion with the bishop.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most agree forgiveness is open; the condition (communion with the bishop) divides Catholics and Orthodox from Protestants.

opinions.position: Compliments hurt him; being praised feeds the pride that could destroy him.
opinions.quote: For they that speak to me [in the way of commendation] scourge me.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today think encouragement is healthy; a minority distrust praise. Fresh and personal: good quiz material ("Being praised does me more harm than good").

opinions.position: The test of true faith is care for widows, orphans, the oppressed, prisoners and the hungry; false teachers show themselves by neglecting them.
opinions.side_note: Care for the poor as proof of faith.
opinions.quote: They have no regard for love; no care for the widow, or the orphan, or the oppressed; of the bond, or of the free; of the hungry, or of the thirsty.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Widely agreed; one-sided.

opinions.topic: new: your life is not your own
opinions.position: A Christian does not belong to himself; he must always be ready to be sent.
opinions.quote: A Christian has not power over himself, but must always be ready for the service of God.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Strong split: modern culture prizes self-ownership; committed believers accept belonging to God. Good quiz item.

opinions.position: Do not look down on a leader because he is young; respect the office, not the age.
opinions.side_note: Contrasts with Irenaeus, who prized mature age (Against Heresies 2.22).
opinions.quote: Now it becomes you also not to treat your bishop too familiarly on account of his youth, but to yield him all reverence
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many think age brings wisdom; others think youth is no bar.

opinions.position: Masters should not despise slaves, but slaves should not expect the church to buy their freedom.
opinions.side_note: A reader-caution item: accepts the institution while insisting on dignity.
opinions.quote: Do not despise either male or female slaves, yet neither let them be puffed up with conceit, but rather let them submit themselves the more, for the glory of God, that they may obtain from God a better liberty. Let them not long to be set free [from slavery] at the public expense, that they be not found slaves to their own desires.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Everyone today rejects slavery; not usable as a quiz statement, but honest background.

opinions.position: It makes no sense to confess Christ and still live by the Jewish law; Christians keep the Lord's Day, not the Sabbath.
opinions.side_note: Contrasts with Justin, who welcomed Jewish believers who kept the law (Dialogue 47).
opinions.quote: It is absurd to profess Christ Jesus, and to Judaize.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Mostly a non-issue for ordinary people today; Messianic Jews and Sabbath-keepers would disagree. Needs care: the tone can read as anti-Jewish.

opinions.position: Put up with everyone the way the Lord puts up with you.
opinions.quote: Bear with all, even as the Lord does with you.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Widely agreed in theory; many think some people should be cut off. Mild split.

opinions.position: Some deep teaching should be held back from beginners, who could be "strangled" by it.
opinions.side_note: Not about pagan learning; about pacing what is taught.
opinions.quote: Am I not able to write to you of heavenly things? But I fear to do so, lest I should inflict injury on you who are but babes [in Christ]. Pardon me in this respect, lest, as not being able to receive [such doctrines], you should be strangled by them.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: some want everything explained openly; others believe in milk before meat.

opinions.position: Someone who corrupts the faith by false teaching "shall go away into everlasting fire", and so will his followers.
opinions.side_note: Side: against universal salvation.
opinions.quote: Such an one becoming defiled [in this way], shall go away into everlasting fire, and so shall every one that hearkens unto him.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many today, inside and outside churches, doubt eternal punishment; traditional Christians affirm it.

sparring.with: Unnamed teachers at Philadelphia who demanded proof from the "archives" (the Old Testament)
sparring.over: Whether the Gospel must be proved from ancient Scripture before it is believed

sparring.with: Docetists (unnamed; he refuses to write their names)
sparring.over: Whether Christ truly had a body and truly suffered; they also abstained from the Eucharist
sparring.source: Letter to the Smyrnaeans, chapters 2-7; Letter to the Trallians, chapter 10

sparring.with: Christians who kept Jewish law and customs ("Judaizers")
sparring.over: Sabbath versus the Lord's Day; living "according to the Jewish law"
sparring.source: Letter to the Magnesians, chapters 8-10; Letter to the Philadelphians, chapter 6

sparring.with: Justin Martyr (not a real exchange: a contrast of their writings)
sparring.over: Ignatius: "It is absurd to profess Christ Jesus, and to Judaize"; Justin, a generation later, would share meals and fellowship with Jewish believers who kept the law, provided they did not force it on others

sparring.with: No recorded quarrel with any named Christian
sparring.over: His surviving writings are seven short letters written in a few weeks; all his named contacts (Polycarp, Onesimus, Burrhus, Crocus) are friends

figures.name: Justin Martyr
figures.dates: c. 100 - c. 165 (beheaded at Rome under the prefect Junius Rusticus)
figures.places: Born at Flavia Neapolis (Nablus) in Samaria; studied in the Greek schools; converted after a talk with an old man in a field by the sea (the place is not named); Eusebius places the Dialogue with Trypho at Ephesus; taught in Rome, living "above one Martinus, at the Timiotinian Bath"
figures.role: Lay teacher and philosopher who kept wearing the philosopher's cloak after becoming a Christian; the first great Christian apologist (writer of defences of the faith to the emperors)
figures.status_note: Saint in the Catholic (1 June) and Eastern Orthodox churches; honoured by Anglicans and Lutherans. Cautions: his language about the Son ("holding Him in the second place", "another God" in the Dialogue) predates Nicene precision and reads as subordinationist to later ears; he held that Christ will reign a thousand years in a rebuilt Jerusalem; the Dialogue with Trypho, though courteous, contains hard words about the Jewish people ("you slew the Christ"). Several works printed under his name are not his: the Hortatory Address to the Greeks, On the Sole Government of God and the Discourse to the Greeks; the fragments On the Resurrection are disputed. The Letter to Diognetus was once credited to him and is not his. The letters of Hadrian, Antoninus and Marcus Aurelius printed after the First Apology include forgeries (the Marcus Aurelius "thundering legion" letter is certainly spurious).
figures.hook: He shopped for a philosophy, walked out on a teacher who asked for his fee up front, met a stranger by the sea who talked him into Christ, and ended up beheaded in Rome after publicly humiliating a Cynic in debate.

stories.story: Before his conversion he went teacher to teacher: a Stoic who "did not know himself" about God; a Peripatetic who after a few days "requested me to settle the fee", so Justin left him as "no philosopher at all"; a proud Pythagorean who turned him away for not knowing music, astronomy and geometry ("I took it rather impatiently"); then the Platonists, until "such was my stupidity, I expected immediately to look upon God".

Walking alone in a field by the sea to think, he was followed by "a certain old man, by no means contemptible in appearance". The old man took apart his Platonism question by question, pointed him to the prophets, walked off, and was never seen again. "But straightway a flame was kindled in my soul."

What first moved him was watching Christians die: "when I was delighting in the doctrines of Plato, and heard the Christians slandered, and saw them fearless of death... perceived that it was impossible that they could be living in wickedness and pleasure."

A Jew named Trypho greeted him in a colonnade because of his philosopher's cloak. When Trypho's friends laughed and jeered, Justin got up to leave, "but he, taking hold of my garment, said I should not accomplish that until I had performed what I promised." They argued for two days and parted friends, Trypho asking him to "remember us as friends when you are gone".

He publicly cross-examined the Cynic philosopher Crescens and wrote that he expected to be "plotted against and fixed to the stake... perhaps by Crescens". His pupil Tatian later said Crescens did plot his death, and Eusebius says he died "in consequence of a plot laid against him by Crescens".
stories.source: Second Apology, chapter 3; Eusebius, Church History 4.16 (quoting Tatian)

stories.story: At his trial the prefect Rusticus asked where Christians met. Justin gave his own address ("I live above one Martinus, at the Timiotinian Bath") and said anyone who came to him heard the truth. Asked his teaching, he said: "I have endeavoured to learn all doctrines; but I have acquiesced at last in the true doctrines, those namely of the Christians." He and six companions were scourged and beheaded.
stories.source: The Martyrdom of Justin and his companions (the Acts of Justin, an early account drawn from the trial record), chapters 1-5

stories.story: He told the emperor of a young Christian in Alexandria who petitioned the governor for permission to be castrated, to prove Christians were not sexually immoral. The governor refused, and "the youth remained single, and was satisfied with his own approving conscience".

He reported a case from Rome: a woman who became a Christian tried to reform her debauched husband, then divorced him; he denounced her as a Christian, and then had her teacher Ptolemaeus arrested. When a bystander named Lucius protested the sentence ("What is the ground of this judgment?"), he was condemned too, and thanked the judge.

temperament.trait: Restless, impatient seeker
temperament.evidence: With the Pythagorean who demanded years of geometry first: "Accordingly I took it rather impatiently... I was not able to endure longer procrastination."

temperament.trait: Playful and courteous
temperament.evidence: The translation marks his first reply to Trypho as a joke: "(In jest.) But who are you, most excellent man?" After two days of argument they wish him a safe voyage, and he leaves "praying for them".

temperament.trait: Combative in public argument
temperament.evidence: He accused Crescens of speaking about what he had not read, said he had "found most convincingly that he, in truth, knows nothing", and offered to repeat the debate before the emperor.

temperament.trait: Blunt honesty; refuses to say one thing and think another
temperament.evidence: "I am not so miserable a fellow, Trypho, as to say one thing and think another."

temperament.trait: Disclaims eloquence
temperament.evidence: He says he quotes Scripture "not that I am anxious to make merely an artful display of words; for I possess no such faculty". Trypho did not believe him.

temperament.trait: Proud to be a Christian, generous to pagan thinkers
temperament.evidence: "I confess that I both boast and with all my strength strive to be found a Christian; not because the teachings of Plato are different from those of Christ, but because they are not in all respects similar."

temperament.trait: Would not stay to be mocked
temperament.evidence: When Trypho's friends "laughed, and shouted in an unseemly manner", he rose to leave and told them to listen in silence or go away.

genuine_lines.quote: and you, you can kill, but not hurt us.
genuine_lines.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Whatever things were rightly said among all men, are the property of us Christians.
genuine_lines.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Reason directs those who are truly pious and philosophical to honour and love only what is true, declining to follow traditional opinions, if these be worthless.
genuine_lines.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: But straightway a flame was kindled in my soul; and a love of the prophets, and of those men who are friends of Christ, possessed me; and while revolving his words in my mind, I found this philosophy alone to be safe and profitable.
genuine_lines.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: for it is in our power, when we are examined, to deny that we are Christians; but we would not live by telling a lie.
genuine_lines.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: I have endeavoured to learn all doctrines; but I have acquiesced at last in the true doctrines, those namely of the Christians, even though they do not please those who hold false opinions.
genuine_lines.work: The Martyrdom of Justin (Acts of Justin, drawn from the trial record)
genuine_lines.translation: M. Dods, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: I am not so miserable a fellow, Trypho, as to say one thing and think another.
genuine_lines.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Wherefore we give thanks when we pay this debt.
genuine_lines.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent

misattributed.line: "What the soul is in the body, Christians are in the world."
misattributed.truth: From the anonymous Letter to Diognetus (chapter 6), once printed among Justin's works because it survived in the same manuscript. Not by Justin.

misattributed.line: Anything quoted from the "Hortatory Address to the Greeks", "On the Sole Government of God" or the "Discourse to the Greeks"
misattributed.truth: Printed under Justin's name (and so listed on New Advent) but generally judged not his. The fragments "On the Resurrection" are disputed.

misattributed.line: The letter of Marcus Aurelius to the Senate crediting Christian prayer for rain (the "thundering legion"), printed at the end of the First Apology
misattributed.truth: A later forgery appended to Justin's text. The rain miracle story itself is old (Eusebius, Church History 5.5, citing Apolinarius and Tertullian), but the letter is not genuine and is not Justin's.

misattributed.line: "Christianity is the only true philosophy" (as a quotation)
misattributed.truth: A fair paraphrase, not his words. What he wrote is "I found this philosophy alone to be safe and profitable" (Dialogue 8).

opinions.position: Every true thing any pagan philosopher or poet said belongs to Christians; Plato and the Stoics had seeds of the truth.
opinions.side_note: Side: pro-learning (the opposite pole from Tertullian, who asked what Athens has to do with Jerusalem).
opinions.quote: Whatever things were rightly said among all men, are the property of us Christians.
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most educated people agree; some Christians are wary of secular philosophy. A good pole against Tertullian.

opinions.position: He tried every school before settling on Christianity, and said so at his own trial.
opinions.side_note: Pro-learning.
opinions.quote: I have endeavoured to learn all doctrines; but I have acquiesced at last in the true doctrines, those namely of the Christians
opinions.translation: M. Dods, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Popular today ("study everything, then decide"). Mostly one-sided.

opinions.position: A truly thoughtful person loves only what is true and drops traditional opinions if they are worthless, even under threat of death.
opinions.side_note: Side: question inherited beliefs.
opinions.quote: Reason directs those who are truly pious and philosophical to honour and love only what is true, declining to follow traditional opinions, if these be worthless.
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today agree strongly; tradition-first believers would add caution. Mild split.

opinions.position: Christ is the Word shared by every race; those who lived by reason before Christ, like Socrates and Heraclitus, were Christians even if called atheists.
opinions.side_note: Side: the good who never heard can belong to Christ.
opinions.quote: and those who lived reasonably are Christians, even though they have been thought atheists; as, among the Greeks, Socrates and Heraclitus, and men like them
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many agree good people outside Christianity are not lost; exclusivist Christians disagree. Strong quiz candidate.

opinions.position: Christians could escape death by denying the faith under questioning, but will not live by a lie; it is impious not to speak the truth in all things.
opinions.side_note: Side: never lie, even to save your life.
opinions.quote: But when we are examined, we make no denial, because we are not conscious of any evil, but count it impious not to speak the truth in all things
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today would lie to save a life; strict truth-tellers are a minority. Good split.

opinions.position: Christians, once killers, no longer make war on their enemies; they have beaten their swords into ploughshares.
opinions.side_note: Side: peaceful, non-violent (describing Christian practice, read as a norm).
opinions.quote: we who formerly used to murder one another do not only now refrain from making war upon our enemies, but also, that we may not lie nor deceive our examiners, willingly die confessing Christ.
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most Christians today accept just war and self-defence; pacifists (Mennonites, Quakers, some Orthodox and Catholics) agree with Justin.

opinions.position: Across the world Christians have traded weapons of war for tools of farming.
opinions.side_note: Same side.
opinions.quote: and we who were filled with war, and mutual slaughter, and every wickedness, have each through the whole earth changed our warlike weapons — our swords into ploughshares, and our spears into implements of tillage— and we cultivate piety, righteousness, philanthropy, faith, and hope
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: As above.

opinions.position: Those who once loved money above everything now pool what they have and share with anyone in need.
opinions.side_note: Side: share possessions.
opinions.quote: we who valued above all things the acquisition of wealth and possessions, now bring what we have into a common stock, and communicate to every one in need
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most admire generosity; few accept a common purse. A split on how far sharing should go.

opinions.position: At every Sunday gathering the well-off give what they choose, and the leader uses it for orphans, widows, the sick, prisoners and strangers.
opinions.side_note: Voluntary giving, not compulsory.
opinions.quote: And they who are well to do, and willing, give what each thinks fit; and what is collected is deposited with the president, who succours the orphans and widows and those who, through sickness or any other cause, are in want, and those who are in bonds and the strangers sojourning among us, and in a word takes care of all who are in need.
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Widely agreed; one-sided.

opinions.position: Rulers should judge by evidence and reason, not rumour or force, and should never punish anyone for a name or a belief alone.
opinions.side_note: Side: against punishing belief. (He did ask that Christians who committed crimes be punished like anyone else.)
opinions.quote: and do not decree death against those who have done no wrong, as you would against enemies.
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Nearly universal agreement today on freedom of belief; the interesting split comes later (Augustine on force).

opinions.topic: new: pay taxes to a hostile state
opinions.position: Christians pay taxes more readily than anyone, worship God alone, and gladly serve the rulers in everything else, even while those rulers persecute them.
opinions.quote: Whence to God alone we render worship, but in other things we gladly serve you, acknowledging you as kings and rulers of men
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most agree taxes should be paid; some think an unjust government forfeits obedience. Mild split.

opinions.topic: new: faith by choice, not by birth
opinions.position: We were born without choosing; baptism is how a person stops being a child "of necessity and of ignorance" and becomes a child "of choice and knowledge".
opinions.side_note: Adult, chosen faith. (He does not discuss infants here.)
opinions.quote: in order that we may not remain the children of necessity and of ignorance, but may become the children of choice and knowledge
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Popular today; people who value inherited faith and infant baptism would put it differently. Good split: "Faith you inherit is not really yours."

opinions.position: Nothing happens by fate; each person freely chooses good or evil and is rewarded or punished for it.
opinions.side_note: Side: strong free will and merit (before Augustine's debates).
opinions.quote: But neither do we affirm that it is by fate that men do what they do, or suffer what they suffer, but that each man by free choice acts rightly or sins
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people believe in free will; determinists and strict Calvinists disagree in different ways. Good quiz item on fate.

opinions.topic: new: everyone knows right from wrong
opinions.position: Every people knows that adultery, fornication and murder are wrong, even while doing them.
opinions.quote: and every race knows that adultery, and fornication, and homicide, and such like, are sinful; and though they all commit such practices, yet they do not escape from the knowledge that they act unrighteously whenever they so do
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many believe in a universal conscience; moral relativists say right and wrong vary by culture.

opinions.position: Anyone who can tell the truth to others and stays silent will be judged by God; that fear is why Christians argue so earnestly.
opinions.side_note: Opposite in spirit to Ignatius's praise of silence.
opinions.quote: every one who can speak the truth, and yet speaks it not, shall be judged by God
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Sharp split: many think religion is private and should not be pressed on others; evangelicals agree with Justin. Strong quiz item.

opinions.position: Christians must not quarrel; they should draw people away from evil by patience and gentleness, as many were won by Christians' honesty in business and patience when cheated.
opinions.side_note: Gentle persuasion.
opinions.quote: For we ought not to strive; neither has He desired us to be imitators of wicked men, but He has exhorted us to lead all men, by patience and gentleness, from shame and the love of evil.
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Widely agreed in principle.

opinions.position: Christians marry only to raise children; otherwise they stay single and chaste.
opinions.side_note: Procreation as the purpose of marriage.
opinions.quote: But whether we marry, it is only that we may bring up children; or whether we decline marriage, we live continently.
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today, including most Christians, see companionship and love as central to marriage. Strong split with a minority.

opinions.position: Those who remarry under human law (after divorce) are sinners in Christ's eyes.
opinions.side_note: Strict on remarriage.
opinions.quote: So that all who, by human law, are twice married, are in the eye of our Master sinners
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most today accept remarriage after divorce; Catholic teaching and some Protestants are strict. Scholars debate whether he meant all second marriages or remarriage after divorce.

opinions.position: He boasts of Christians who have kept chaste from childhood to sixty or seventy, from every nation.
opinions.side_note: Pro-celibacy, as an honour, not a rule.
opinions.quote: And many, both men and women, who have been Christ's disciples from childhood, remain pure at the age of sixty or seventy years; and I boast that I could produce such from every race of men.
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Few today treat lifelong virginity as an achievement; Catholic and Orthodox monastics would.

opinions.position: Exposing (abandoning) newborn babies is wicked: most end up in prostitution, and some die, making the parents murderers.
opinions.side_note: The ancient form of the protection-of-infants question.
opinions.quote: we have been taught that to expose newly-born children is the part of wicked men
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Everyone today condemns abandoning babies; the modern parallel (abortion) is heavily contested, but drawing it would be our inference, not his.

opinions.position: Christians must not kill themselves to get to God sooner, but when questioned they confess without fear.
opinions.side_note: A middle position between Ignatius's eagerness and flight.
opinions.quote: If, then, we all kill ourselves we shall become the cause, as far as in us lies, why no one should be born, or instructed in the divine doctrines, or even why the human race should not exist; and we shall, if we so act, be ourselves acting in opposition to the will of God.
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Agreed by almost all; useful only as context.

opinions.topic: new: welcome believers with different practices
opinions.position: Jewish believers who keep the law of Moses but do not force it on others should be treated "as kinsmen and brethren"; he disagrees with Christians who refuse to eat or associate with them.
opinions.side_note: Related to "pure-church": inclusive on practice, firm on Christ.
opinions.quote: then I hold that we ought to join ourselves to such, and associate with them in all things as kinsmen and brethren
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most today favour this kind of tolerance; stricter groups draw firmer lines. Useful pole against Ignatius.

opinions.topic: new: a thousand-year reign on earth
opinions.position: Christ will reign for a thousand years in a rebuilt Jerusalem after the resurrection, though he admits many true Christians think otherwise.
opinions.side_note: Literal millennium, held charitably.
opinions.quote: But I and others, who are right-minded Christians on all points, are assured that there will be a resurrection of the dead, and a thousand years in Jerusalem, which will then be built, adorned, and enlarged
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Many evangelicals hold a literal millennium; Catholics, Orthodox and most mainline Protestants do not. Most non-Christians have no view.

opinions.position: The wicked will be punished in their bodies with everlasting punishment, not merely for a thousand years as Plato said.
opinions.side_note: Side: against universal salvation.
opinions.quote: and upon the wicked in the same bodies united again to their spirits which are now to undergo everlasting punishment; and not only, as Plato said, for a period of a thousand years
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many doubt eternal punishment; traditional Christians affirm it.

opinions.position: Christians in his own day drive out demons in Jesus's name where other exorcists fail, and prophetic gifts remain in the Church.
opinions.side_note: Side: the gifts continue. The exorcism claim is in the Second Apology, chapter 6.
opinions.quote: For the prophetical gifts remain with us, even to the present time.
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Pentecostals and charismatics agree; cessationist Protestants and sceptics disagree. Strong split.

opinions.position: God needs no sacrifices; the fitting worship is to use what He made for ourselves and for those in need, and to thank Him for health, the qualities of things and the changing seasons.
opinions.side_note: Creation is good and to be received with thanks.
opinions.quote: but to use it for ourselves and those who need, and with gratitude to Him to offer thanks by invocations and hymns for our creation, and for all the means of health, and for the various qualities of the different kinds of things, and for the changes of the seasons
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Widely agreed.

opinions.position: Death is a debt everyone owes; Christians give thanks when they pay it.
opinions.side_note: Related to "grief".
opinions.quote: were not death a debt due by every man that is born. Wherefore we give thanks when we pay this debt.
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people fear death or grieve it; a calm, grateful view is a minority. Good personal item.

opinions.position: Before his conversion he loved solitary walks for thinking; the old man who converted him asked whether he was "a philologian, but no lover of deeds or of truth".
opinions.side_note: Mixed: he loved solitude, but the story turns on its limits. This is his pre-Christian self as he tells it.
opinions.quote: I delight in such walks, where my attention is not distracted, for converse with myself is uninterrupted
opinions.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Introverts will recognise themselves; weak as a position statement.

sparring.with: Crescens the Cynic (a pagan philosopher, not a Christian)
sparring.over: Crescens called Christians atheists before crowds; Justin cross-examined him in public and expected Crescens to get him killed. Tatian and Eusebius say he did.
sparring.source: Second Apology, chapter 3; Eusebius, Church History 4.16

sparring.over: Marcion taught a higher god than the Creator; Justin says he "has caused many of every nation to speak blasphemies" and mentions his own lost treatise against all heresies.

sparring.with: Christians who refused fellowship with law-keeping Jewish believers
sparring.over: Whether to eat with and welcome them; "I do not agree with them."

sparring.with: Christians who rejected the thousand-year reign
sparring.over: He admits "many who belong to the pure and pious faith, and are true Christians, think otherwise" but holds his view.

sparring.with: Tatian, his own pupil (after Justin's death)
sparring.over: Tatian left the Church, condemned marriage and founded the Encratites; Irenaeus says "as long as he continued with him he expressed no such views".
sparring.source: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 1.28.1; Eusebius, Church History 4.29

sparring.with: Trypho (a Jewish teacher; a friendly debate, not a Christian quarrel)
sparring.over: Whether Jesus is the Christ and whether the Law still binds; two days of argument ending in friendship

portraits.artist: Theophanes the Cretan (Stavronikita Monastery, Mount Athos)

portraits.date: first half of the 16th century (Russia; Ikonen-Museum Recklinghausen)
