figures.name: Irenaeus of Lyons
figures.places: Grew up in Asia Minor (probably Smyrna), where as a boy he heard Polycarp; presbyter and then bishop of Lugdunum (Lyons) in Gaul; visited Rome
figures.role: Bishop of Lyons after the persecution of 177; author of Against Heresies (the "Exposure and Overthrow of Knowledge Falsely So Called") and the Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching; peacemaker in the Easter dispute
figures.status_note: Saint in the Catholic (28 June) and Eastern Orthodox (23 August) churches; declared a Doctor of the Church ("Doctor of Unity") by Pope Francis in 2022. Cautions: he taught a literal thousand-year kingdom on a renewed earth, and argued that Jesus was over forty, nearly fifty, when He died (Against Heresies 2.22), both minority views later. Against Heresies survives whole only in an early Latin translation (plus Greek excerpts and Armenian books 4-5); the Demonstration survives only in Armenian. He is honoured as a martyr, but Eusebius, who reports much about him, says nothing of a martyrdom; the tradition appears in later sources (for example Gregory of Tours, 6th century), so it is uncertain. Four "fragments of Irenaeus" published by C. M. Pfaff in 1715 are forgeries made by Pfaff himself.
figures.hook: To mock a sect's grand names for the hidden powers of the universe, he coined his own: "a power which I term a Gourd", with "Utter-Emptiness", "the Cucumber" and "a Melon".

stories.story: As a boy in Smyrna he sat under Polycarp, who had known the apostle John. Decades later he wrote that he remembered it better than recent years: "I am able to describe the very place in which the blessed Polycarp sat as he discoursed, and his goings out and his comings in." He stored the words "not on paper, but in my heart".
stories.source: Letter to Florinus, preserved in Eusebius, Church History 5.20

stories.story: In 177 the Christians of Lyons and Vienne sent him to Rome with a letter for bishop Eleutherus, praising him as "zealous for the covenant of Christ". The persecution killed many of them, among them the 90-year-old bishop Pothinus, and Irenaeus succeeded him as bishop.

When Pope Victor of Rome tried to excommunicate all the churches of Asia for keeping Easter on a different day, Irenaeus wrote to rebuke him, reminding him that Polycarp and Pope Anicetus had disagreed about the same thing and still shared the Eucharist and "parted from each other in peace". Eusebius says he "truly was well named, became a peacemaker in this matter".

He parodied a Gnostic teacher's invented names for the first powers of the universe ("Monotes", "Henotes"), crying "Iu, Iu! Pheu, Pheu!" and proposing instead a first principle called "a Gourd", with "Utter-Emptiness", "the Cucumber" and "a Melon", which "brought forth the remaining multitude of the delirious melons of Valentinus".

He ended one of his books with a solemn charge to anyone copying it: "I adjure you who may copy this book, by our Lord Jesus Christ... to compare what you shall write, and correct it carefully by this manuscript." Eusebius copied it out as a model of "painstaking carefulness".
stories.source: On the Ogdoad, preserved in Eusebius, Church History 5.20

stories.story: He wrote to Florinus, a man he had known in Polycarp's circle who had become a Roman presbyter and drifted toward Valentinian teaching: "These doctrines, O Florinus, to speak mildly, are not of sound judgment." He also urged Pope Victor to expel Florinus's books from the Roman church.
stories.source: Eusebius, Church History 5.20; Fragment 51 (letter to Victor, preserved in Syriac)

stories.story: He passed on Polycarp's stories: that the apostle John fled a bath-house shouting "Let us fly, lest even the bath-house fall down" because the heretic Cerinthus was inside, and that Polycarp, when Marcion asked "Do you know me?", answered "I do know you, the first-born of Satan."

He argued that Jesus was not about thirty when He died but past forty, "not far from" fifty, citing John 8:57 ("You are not yet fifty years old") and "all the elders" who knew John, so that Christ would sanctify every age of life, old age included.

temperament.trait: Sarcastic wit against pretension
temperament.evidence: The Gourd-and-Melon parody; he also exclaims "O you trifling sophists!" and mocks those who would count the hairs on everyone's head to prove their system.

temperament.trait: Modest about his own style, living among the Celts
temperament.evidence: "You will not expect from me, who am resident among the Keltæ, and am accustomed for the most part to use a barbarous dialect, any display of rhetoric, which I have never learned."

temperament.trait: Peacemaker, true to his name
temperament.evidence: Eusebius: "Irenæus, who truly was well named, became a peacemaker in this matter, exhorting and negotiating in this way in behalf of the peace of the churches."

temperament.trait: Loves his opponents while fighting them
temperament.evidence: "We pray for these things on their behalf, loving them better than they seem to love themselves... it shall not weary us, to endeavour with all our might to stretch out the hand unto them."

temperament.trait: Meticulous and careful
temperament.evidence: His adjuration to copyists to check their copy against his manuscript, which Eusebius cites as an example of "painstaking carefulness".

temperament.trait: Loyal to his teachers; long, vivid memory
temperament.evidence: "For what boys learn, growing with their mind, becomes joined with it."
temperament.source: Letter to Florinus, in Eusebius, Church History 5.20.6

temperament.trait: Blunt with an old acquaintance
temperament.evidence: "These doctrines, O Florinus, to speak mildly, are not of sound judgment."

genuine_lines.quote: For the glory of God is a living man; and the life of man consists in beholding God.
genuine_lines.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: who did, through His transcendent love, become what we are, that He might bring us to be even what He is Himself.
genuine_lines.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: For where the Church is, there is the Spirit of God; and where the Spirit of God is, there is the Church, and every kind of grace
genuine_lines.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: and the disagreement in regard to the fast confirms the agreement in the faith.
genuine_lines.work: Letter to Pope Victor, preserved in Eusebius, Church History
genuine_lines.translation: A. C. McGiffert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 1 (1890), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Offer to Him your heart in a soft and tractable state, and preserve the form in which the Creator has fashioned you, having moisture in yourself, lest, by becoming hardened, you lose the impressions of His fingers.
genuine_lines.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: We pray for these things on their behalf, loving them better than they seem to love themselves.
genuine_lines.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: so that God should for ever teach, and man should for ever learn the things taught him by God
genuine_lines.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: For what boys learn, growing with their mind, becomes joined with it
genuine_lines.work: Letter to Florinus, preserved in Eusebius, Church History
genuine_lines.translation: A. C. McGiffert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 1 (1890), as revised for New Advent

misattributed.line: "The glory of God is man fully alive."
misattributed.truth: A popular paraphrase that drops half the sentence. Against Heresies 4.20.7 reads: "For the glory of God is a living man; and the life of man consists in beholding God." The point is that life comes from seeing God, not self-fulfilment.

misattributed.line: Four "fragments of Irenaeus" beginning "True knowledge, then, consists in the understanding of Christ", "Those who have become acquainted with the secondary constitutions of the apostles", "The apostles ordained, that we should not judge any one in respect to meat or drink... Whence then these contentions? Whence these schisms?" and "Christ, who was called the Son of God before the ages" (numbered 36-39 on the New Advent fragments page)
misattributed.truth: Published by C. M. Pfaff in 1715 "ostensibly from a Turin manuscript". The Catholic Encyclopedia (article "St. Irenaeus") reports that Funk proved them apocryphal and Harnack showed that Pfaff himself fabricated them. The matching of these four texts to Pfaff's four is from standard knowledge, not re-checked against Pfaff's edition here.

misattributed.line: "As long as any one has the means of doing good to his neighbours, and does not do so, he shall be reckoned a stranger to the love of the Lord." and "The business of the Christian is nothing else than to be ever preparing for death."
misattributed.truth: Printed as Irenaeus fragments 4 and 11, but they come from late anthologies (catenae and florilegia) and their attribution is uncertain. Do not build a result on them.

misattributed.line: The saying that in the kingdom "vines shall grow, each having ten thousand branches" and every grape will give twenty-five measures of wine, which Irenaeus credits to the Lord through "the elders who saw John" and Papias
misattributed.truth: Irenaeus really wrote this (Against Heresies 5.33.3), but the saying is not in the Gospels; a close parallel is in the Jewish apocalypse 2 Baruch 29:5. Present it as what Irenaeus believed Jesus said, not as a saying of Jesus.
His martyrdom is traditional but not attested by Eusebius; it is reported in later sources and is uncertain.

opinions.position: Churches that keep Easter or fasts differently should stay in communion; different customs even prove the shared faith. Do not cut off whole churches over custom.
opinions.side_note: Related to "pure-church": against excommunicating over non-essentials. He rebuked the bishop of Rome for doing it.
opinions.quote: Yet all of these lived none the less in peace, and we also live in peace with one another; and the disagreement in regard to the fast confirms the agreement in the faith.
opinions.work: Letter to Pope Victor, in Eusebius, Church History
opinions.translation: A. C. McGiffert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 1 (1890), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today agree differences in practice should not divide; some traditionalists and strict denominations think practice and doctrine go together. Good item.

opinions.position: No reform people could achieve by breaking away is worth the damage done by the split.
opinions.side_note: Strongly anti-schism.
opinions.quote: For no reformation of so great importance can be effected by them, as will compensate for the mischief arising from their schism.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Sharply split: Catholics and Orthodox largely agree; the Protestant tradition was born of the opposite judgment, and many people today leave churches freely. Excellent quiz statement ("Staying together matters more than getting everything right").

opinions.position: When Christians disagree on an important question, go back to the oldest churches the apostles taught and learn what they hold.
opinions.quote: Suppose there arise a dispute relative to some important question among us, should we not have recourse to the most ancient Churches with which the apostles held constant intercourse, and learn from them what is certain and clear in regard to the present question?
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split between tradition-first Christians (Catholic, Orthodox) and Scripture-alone or individual-judgment Christians; most non-religious people would reject appeals to tradition.

opinions.position: Better to be simple and unlettered and near to God by love than learned and proud and led into blasphemy.
opinions.side_note: Side: wary of speculative learning (he does not reject knowledge of God).
opinions.quote: It is therefore better and more profitable to belong to the simple and unlettered class, and by means of love to attain to nearness to God
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many value simple faith; many others think education and hard questions make faith stronger. Pole against Justin and Clement.

opinions.position: Some questions (what God did before creation, where matter came from, why some creatures sinned) must be left to God; it is no shame to say that only God knows.
opinions.side_note: Side: accept limits on questions.
opinions.quote: If, for instance, any one asks, What was God doing before He made the world? we reply that the answer to such a question lies with God Himself.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: curious and sceptical people want every question pursued; many believers are content with mystery.

opinions.position: The gladiator shows are "that bloody spectacle hateful both to God and men"; attending them marks false Christians.
opinions.side_note: Side: against the shows.
opinions.quote: that bloody spectacle hateful both to God and men, in which gladiators either fight with wild beasts, or singly encounter one another
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Everyone today condemns gladiator killing; the live split is violent entertainment in general (films, games, combat sports).

opinions.position: Forbidding marriage or meat is ingratitude to the God who made male and female and all things.
opinions.side_note: Side: against rigorist asceticism (Tatian and the Encratites).
opinions.quote: Some of those reckoned among them have also introduced abstinence from animal food, thus proving themselves ungrateful to God, who formed all things.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most agree marriage is good; vegetarians and vegans today usually abstain for ethical reasons he did not consider. Mild split.

opinions.position: Preaching against marriage insults the Creator who made male and female to bring new people into the world.
opinions.side_note: Pro-marriage.
opinions.quote: preached against marriage, thus setting aside the original creation of God, and indirectly blaming Him who made the male and female for the propagation of the human race
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Widely agreed; one-sided today.

opinions.position: Miracles continue in the Church of his day: exorcism, prophecy, healing by laying on of hands, even raising the dead, all without fee.
opinions.side_note: Side: gifts continue.
opinions.quote: Yea, moreover, as I have said, the dead even have been raised up, and remained among us for many years.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Pentecostals and charismatics agree; sceptics and cessationists doubt. Strong split.

opinions.position: Many in the Church prophesy and "speak all kinds of languages" through the Spirit.
opinions.side_note: Side: gifts continue, including tongues.
opinions.quote: In like manner we do also hear many brethren in the Church, who possess prophetic gifts, and who through the Spirit speak all kinds of languages
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: As above.

opinions.position: Keep reaching out to those in error and pray for them; true love is a severe remedy, but offered out of love.
opinions.side_note: Firm but loving; contrasts with the Polycarp stories he also tells ("first-born of Satan").
opinions.quote: Wherefore it shall not weary us, to endeavour with all our might to stretch out the hand unto them.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Widely admired; some think arguing with the wrong-headed is pointless. Mild split.

opinions.position: The apostles and their disciples had a horror of even talking with those who corrupted the truth.
opinions.side_note: Stated approvingly after the Polycarp and John stories; his own practice was to keep writing to them.
opinions.quote: Such was the horror which the apostles and their disciples had against holding even verbal communication with any corrupters of the truth
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most today value dialogue; separatist Christians agree with the principle.

opinions.position: God made people free; He never forces anyone to obey, but counsels all.
opinions.side_note: Side: free will (without the Augustinian questions later raised).
opinions.quote: For there is no coercion with God, but a good will [towards us] is present with Him continually.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people agree; strict predestinarians would object.

opinions.topic: new: people are made to grow
opinions.position: God made humans like infants, able to grow into perfection over time; demanding to be perfect at once is ingratitude.
opinions.quote: but the lord, that is, man, was (but) small; for he was a child; and it was necessary that he should grow, and so come to (his) perfection.
opinions.translation: J. Armitage Robinson, The Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching (SPCK, 1920), from the Armenian; transcribed on tertullian.org
opinions.today: Popular today ("life is growth"); few would disagree, though some Christians stress a fall from original perfection instead.

opinions.topic: new: we learn good by knowing evil
opinions.position: People learn to choose good by experiencing its opposite; without knowing the bitter, you could not really grasp the good.
opinions.side_note: A hopeful reading of failure and suffering.
opinions.quote: But how, if he had no knowledge of the contrary, could he have had instruction in that which is good?
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Many agree mistakes teach; others think evil is never needed to learn good. Good personal item.

opinions.position: Mature age is "more necessary and more honourable than any other"; Christ lived into it to sanctify every stage of life.
opinions.side_note: Contrasts with Ignatius defending a young bishop.
opinions.quote: robbing Him of that age which is both more necessary and more honourable than any other; that more advanced age, I mean, during which also as a teacher He excelled all others
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: youth-focused culture versus respect for elders. Personal and fresh.

opinions.position: All our property was gained in a tainted world (trade, inheritance, profit); what makes it righteous is using it for the Lord and giving it away.
opinions.side_note: Moderate: keep and use wealth, but give.
opinions.quote: For whatsoever we acquired from unrighteousness when we were heathen, we are proved righteous, when we have become believers, by applying it to the Lord's advantage.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most Christians today hold something like this; radical-poverty Christians would push further.

opinions.position: Christ replaced the tithe with sharing all we have with the poor, and even giving freely to those who take our goods.
opinions.side_note: Radical-sounding alongside the moderate view above.
opinions.quote: and not merely to be liberal givers and bestowers, but even that we should present a gratuitous gift to those who take away our goods.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Few practise it; many admire it.

opinions.position: Government is appointed by God, not the devil, so that people "may not eat each other up like fishes"; rulers who act unjustly will perish under God's judgment.
opinions.side_note: Pro-government, with limits.
opinions.quote: Earthly rule, therefore, has been appointed by God for the benefit of nations, and not by the devil, who is never at rest at all, nay, who does not love to see even nations conducting themselves after a quiet manner, so that under the fear of human rule, men may not eat each other up like fishes
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many distrust government as such; others see it as a God-given necessity.

opinions.topic: new: the Roman peace is a gift
opinions.position: Through the Romans "the world is at peace", and Christians can travel roads and seas without fear.
opinions.side_note: A positive view of the pagan empire, even while it persecuted.
opinions.quote: through their instrumentality the world is at peace, and we walk on the highways without fear, and sail where we will
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Background rather than a quiz item.

opinions.position: The Gospel has made nations beat swords into ploughshares; Christians no longer know how to fight and, when struck, turn the other cheek.
opinions.side_note: Peaceful; spoken as fulfilled prophecy about Christians.
opinions.quote: that these [nations] did form the swords and war-lances into ploughshares, and changed them into pruning-hooks for reaping the grain, [that is], into instruments used for peaceful purposes, and that they are now unaccustomed to fighting, but when smitten, offer also the other cheek
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: As with Justin: most Christians today accept just war; pacifists agree.

opinions.position: Those who choose to leave God receive the separation they chose; since God's good things are eternal, their loss is eternal too.
opinions.side_note: Side: against universal salvation; hell as self-chosen loss.
opinions.quote: But on as many as, according to their own choice, depart from God, He inflicts that separation from Himself which they have chosen of their own accord.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split; the "self-chosen separation" framing appeals to many who reject a punishing God.

opinions.position: Christ came not only for those alive in his day but for all who from the beginning feared and loved God and did right by their neighbours.
opinions.side_note: Mainly about the righteous of Israel before Christ (he adds "and have earnestly desired to see Christ").
opinions.quote: For it was not merely for those who believed on Him in the time of Tiberius Cæsar that Christ came, nor did the Father exercise His providence for the men only who are now alive, but for all men altogether, who from the beginning, according to their capacity, in their generation have both feared and loved God, and practised justice and piety towards their neighbours
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split, as with Justin; Irenaeus is narrower than Justin.

opinions.position: Prophecies of a renewed earth must be read literally; people who allegorize them contradict themselves.
opinions.side_note: Side: literal reading of prophecy (against the allegorists).
opinions.quote: If, however, any shall endeavour to allegorize [prophecies] of this kind, they shall not be found consistent with themselves in all points
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split between literal and symbolic readers of prophecy.

opinions.position: The righteous will be rewarded in this same creation, renewed, where they suffered: the world is not to be escaped but restored.
opinions.side_note: Strongly pro-creation.
opinions.quote: For it is just that in that very creation in which they toiled or were afflicted, being proved in every way by suffering, they should receive the reward of their suffering
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Many Christians picture heaven as elsewhere; the "renewed earth" view is growing. Good item.

opinions.position: In the coming kingdom creation will overflow "with an abundance of all kinds of food"; the good things of the earth are part of the reward.
opinions.side_note: Pro-enjoyment of creation's goods.
opinions.quote: when also the creation, having been renovated and set free, shall fructify with an abundance of all kinds of food
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Many find it attractive; others picture heaven as purely spiritual.

opinions.position: There can be neither more nor fewer than four Gospels.
opinions.side_note: The earliest firm statement of the four-Gospel canon.
opinions.quote: It is not possible that the Gospels can be either more or fewer in number than they are.
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Christians agree; some popular writers promote "lost gospels". Too technical for most players.

opinions.position: He urged the bishop of Rome to expel from the church the writings of a presbyter teaching error, because they were a stumbling-block to simple believers.
opinions.side_note: Pro-censorship within the church.
opinions.quote: I call your attention to them, that for the sake of your reputation you may expel these writings from among you, as bringing disgrace upon you
opinions.work: Letter to Victor about Florinus (Syriac fragment)
opinions.location: Fragment 51 in the Ante-Nicene Fathers numbering
opinions.translation: A. Roberts, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Sharply split: most today dislike banning books; many churches still decide what their teachers may teach.

opinions.position: God gives immortality both to those who kept faith from the beginning and to those who came back by repentance.
opinions.side_note: Side: repentance is real and welcomed.
opinions.quote: some from the beginning [of their Christian course], and others from [the date of] their repentance
opinions.translation: A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Widely agreed.

sparring.over: Victor excommunicated the churches of Asia for keeping Easter on the 14th of Nisan; Irenaeus rebuked him and urged peace, citing Polycarp and Anicetus

sparring.with: Florinus, a Roman presbyter he had known in Polycarp's circle
sparring.over: Florinus leaned toward Valentinian teaching and the idea that God is the author of evil; Irenaeus wrote "On the Monarchy" and "On the Ogdoad" against him and urged Victor to expel his books
A schism at Rome (probably over Easter); Irenaeus wrote to him "On Schism"
Tatian condemned marriage and meat and denied Adam's salvation; Irenaeus calls him "puffed up by the thought of being a teacher"

sparring.with: Valentinus, Ptolemaeus, Marcus and the Valentinian school
sparring.over: Secret knowledge, a lower Creator, thirty Aeons, salvation by nature not conduct; the target of all five books
Marcion split God into a just Creator and a good Father and cut the Scriptures; Irenaeus answers that God is both just and good
Eusebius blamed Papias, "of very limited understanding", for leading Fathers "as for instance Irenæus" into the literal thousand-year kingdom

notes: Every quote in genuine_lines and opinions was cut by script from the page at its url and re-checked against a fresh download. New Advent wraps many words (for example "Christ Jesus", "God") in inline links: strip tags WITHOUT inserting spaces, as a browser does, before matching, or matches fail on stray spaces before commas.
Quotes stop short of the Scripture references New Advent prints inline (for example "Matthew 5:39"), so no quote contains one.
Each opinion carries an extra field, today, saying how people now would split on it.
